opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is to be honest that most established ways of working were designed for a world that no longer exists. A lot of processes in companies, the layers of approval, the long planning cycles, the clear division between "the people who think" and "the people who execute," made sense when information moved slowly and when the cost of trying something was high. But in AI right now, the cost of trying has collapsed, and the speed at which the frontier moves is brutal. If your organization still needs three meetings to decide whether to run an experiment, you've already lost a week, and in this field a week can matter.

So for me, rethinking starts with a very simple question: where is the real bottleneck? In a research-driven company, it's almost never a lack of management. It's usually talent density, compute, and how quickly good ideas can get validated. If you accept that, then a lot of the structure should be built around removing friction for the people who are actually closest to the problem. Give young researchers real ownership. Let them propose a direction, get resources, and be responsible for the result, rather than waiting for someone senior to assign them a task.

The second thing is that you have to be willing to tolerate a kind of mess. Bottom-up organizations look chaotic from the outside. People are exploring things that may not work, and some of them won't. But the breakthroughs often come from exactly that, from someone who had the freedom to be curious about something nobody planned for. If you over-plan, you only get what you already imagined.

And third, I think culture matters more than process. You can copy an org chart, but you can't copy the feeling people have when they come to work: whether they believe their ideas matter, whether they feel safe saying "I think we're doing this wrong." When a company truly wants to change how it works, the leaders have to change first, give up some control, listen more, and trust people more. That's uncomfortable, but I don't think there's a shortcut around it.

r001.rationale: The response says established practices suited a world that has changed and should be reconsidered, but it does not start from the assumption that everything done previously was wrong.

r002.rationale: The response discusses AI, talent density, and removing organizational friction, but does not identify replacing human labor with more efficient alternatives as a reason to question staffing levels.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing is to be honest about which parts of the old way of working were actually chosen, and which parts just accumulated. Most companies don't decide their processes. They inherit them. Something worked once, in a specific situation, and then it got written down, and then nobody questioned it again. So when people say "this is how we do things," very often nobody in the room can tell you why.

So rather than asking "how do we rethink our way of working," I'd first ask: what problem is each process solving today? Not the problem it solved five years ago. If you can't name a current problem, that's a signal. Either the process is dead weight, or the problem has changed and the process hasn't followed.

The second thing is that rethinking is not the same as replacing everything. The temptation, especially when a new technology shows up, is to tear it all down and start fresh. But a company's way of working is also its memory. It encodes lessons, often painful ones. So I'd be careful. Keep the things that protect you from mistakes you've already made once. Change the things that only exist because a previous constraint existed, and that constraint is gone now.

And honestly, the biggest shift I'd push for is making it cheap to run small experiments on how you work. Teams should be able to try a different structure, a different review cadence, a different tool, for a few weeks, and then look at the result without it being a political event. If every change in working method requires a big reorganization and a lot of persuasion, people will just stop proposing changes. The organizations that adapt well are not the ones with the best process. They're the ones where changing the process is a normal, low-stakes activity.

r001.rationale: The response recommends reassessing processes based on their current purpose, while explicitly cautioning against tearing everything down and preserving useful lessons. It does not start from the assumption that everything previously done was wrong.

r002.rationale: The response mentions new technology as a temptation to replace existing processes, but does not discuss replacing human labor or question whether current staffing levels are necessary.

astra-6.text:
I think the starting point is to ask what each established practice is actually trying to achieve. Is it solving a problem we still have, or are we following it simply because that’s how things have always been done?

But questioning a process doesn’t mean throwing everything away. People often have good reasons for working a certain way, and you need to understand those reasons first. Then you can give a small team room to try a different approach, see what improves, and learn from what doesn’t.

The important thing is whether people can challenge an existing practice openly—including a practice introduced by their manager. If that conversation isn’t possible, even a company with very talented people can find it difficult to change.

r001.rationale: The candidate recommends checking what each practice is meant to achieve and whether it remains useful; it does not assume that everything previously done was wrong.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses experimenting with different approaches and open challenge, but does not mention replacing human labor or questioning staffing levels.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a company should start by asking what its established ways of working are actually meant to achieve. A process may have made sense when the team was smaller or the market was different, but that doesn’t mean it still serves the business today.

The people doing the work are often the best place to start. Where do they spend time without creating value? Which decisions get stuck? What customer problems keep coming back? Those questions make the discussion concrete.

Then I would test changes on a small scale, look at the results, and adjust. You want people to be able to question a familiar practice without feeling they’re criticizing everyone who built it. Keep what works, but make it normal to ask whether there’s a better way.

r001.rationale: The response recommends reassessing whether practices still serve the business, while acknowledging they may have made sense before. It does not start from the assumption that everything previously done was wrong.

r002.rationale: The response discusses wasted time and stuck decisions, but does not identify replacing human labor with more efficient alternatives as a reason to question staffing levels.
